1:
Everything turns on how wide the word earth is meant to be, and the answers cover the range. Wesley takes it narrowly for the land of Canaan, wasted first by the Assyrians and then by the Chaldeans. Clarke keeps it national too, making the world here the same as the land, the kingdoms of Judah and Israel. Henry argues the other way from usage: where the word means one particular country it almost always has something joined to it saying which, and since nothing does here he sees no reason to narrow it. Ellicott agrees that the Hebrew admits land but thinks the wider sense predominates, since the next verse pairs it with world. Gill rehearses the options, from the captivity of the ten tribes to the Maccabean age, and settles on the papal and antichristian states, the chapter's close reaching to the destruction of the whole world.

Calvin places the chapter rather than defining the word. He takes it as the conclusion of everything said since the thirteenth chapter, where destruction was foretold for Jews and Moabites and Assyrians and Egyptians in turn, so that the prophet, having surveyed all the countries known to his people, now gives a brief summary of the whole. He rejects one reading firmly: those who take it of the whole world but refer it to the last day are offering, in his judgment, an excessively forced interpretation. Clarke supplies the same placement from the other side, noting that the fate of city after city has been denounced from the thirteenth chapter to the twenty-third, and that the prophet now turns the judgment on God's own people.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the genre instead, and find only one parallel for it in the Old Testament. Such prophecies start from circumstances that look sharply defined historically but vanish like will-o'-the-wisps as soon as one tries to follow and seize them, because the prophet takes hold of their root idea, carries it beyond its outward historical form, and uses it as an emblem of far-off events. They add the critical history, that most modern critics have denied these four chapters to the prophet, and that one reversed himself between editions on opposite grounds; and they refuse the test being applied, calling it another of the will-o'-the-wisps already mentioned.

The levelling of ranks in the second verse produces the chapter's most unexpected inference. Calvin reasons backwards from the curse: since the prophet reckons this confusion among the judgments of God, and treats the loss of all distinction between people and priest as a terrible display of vengeance, we ought to conclude how much God is pleased with regular government, and what a privilege its preservation is, for when it is taken away the life of man differs little from the sustenance of cattle and beasts of prey. Wesley reads the same clauses as an equalising in beggary and slavery. Ellicott hears something more local in the last pairs, a trace of indignation at a people already on the way to becoming a nation of money lenders.

The reason for the desolation is given at last, and the covenant named is not the obvious one. Ellicott points out that the verb translated defiled is used elsewhere of blood-guiltiness and of impurity, so it covers every sin which desecrates humanity, and takes the everlasting covenant broken here to be the one made with Noah, making the charge universal rather than national. Clarke notes that the versions read the law in the singular. Keil and Delitzsch render the three charges as transgressing revelations, setting the ordinance at nought and breaking the everlasting covenant. Gill offers an alternative sense for the verb, that the earth plays the hypocrite, promising fruit and bringing none. Calvin takes the lofty ones as men of rank, whose fall is the more wonderful.
7:
The failed vintage is read as a picture and as a charge. Ellicott takes each feature as part of one scene: the vine scorched by the fire of the curse, no wine in the press, the song of the grape-gatherers hushed, those gatherers being proverbially the type of the merry-hearted. Calvin makes it an indictment of luxury: the prophet surveys their intemperance because amid such abundance they proudly disobeyed, and he refuses to keep the fault local, since it is universally found that those who enjoy abundance rebel against God and indulge themselves too freely. He adds that the prophet speaks of the future as though present, to set it more clearly before their eyes. Wesley explains the grief attributed to senseless things as a figure usual in all authors.

Calvin is careful not to let the passage condemn more than it should. To drink wine is not in itself evil, since God appointed it for man's use, and what is described here is the banquet of drunkards, full of licentiousness and insolence; the want threatened is what men bring on themselves when by luxury they turn God's goodness to a bad use. On the bitterness he observes that sorrow deprives a man of relish for what he eats and drinks, so abundance of wine will not be enjoyed. Wesley says the same in a phrase, that it is bitter because of the fears and miseries mixed with it. Clarke identifies the strong drink as palm wine, and Ellicott renders the clause literally as in their song they drink no wine.

The ruined city divides them by identification and unites them on the word. Ellicott renders it the city of chaos, the term used of the earth before it was formed, so the world is cast back out of its cosmos into its primeval chaos; and the houses are shut up not because their gates are barred but because their own ruins block the entrance. Calvin applies it chiefly to Jerusalem while allowing it reaches other cities, and prefers to read the name from their crimes rather than their punishment: a city in which nothing is regular, because justice and good government have been banished from it. Wesley takes the singular collectively for Jerusalem and other cities, and Gill for mystical Babylon.

Two small textual quarrels run through these verses. At the ceasing of mirth Clarke reports manuscripts and versions reading pride where the received text has noise. At the darkening of joy he proposes another change, transposing a letter to give passed away instead of darkened; Ellicott defends the received word, since the English verb exactly expresses a Hebrew term used of the gloom of sunset, the light of joy passing into the blackness of darkness. Ellicott also relocates the crying, taking the noun for an open place outside rather than inside the walls, so men weep in the fields because there is no vintage. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the whole as the judging of the world with its pleasure, and of the world's city where both its power and its pleasure were concentrated.

Then mercy is remembered in the middle of wrath, and Henry works the figure carefully. The shaking of an olive tree and the gleaning grapes measure the remnant, a few here and there who escape the common calamity and can sit down on the ruins of all their creature comforts and still rejoice. He notes two things the figure supplies: they are dispersed and at a distance from one another, like the last olives on a tree, and they are concealed under the leaves, so the Lord knows those who are his though the world does not. Gill reads the same verse of the judgment falling throughout the whole antichristian jurisdiction.
14:
The song that breaks in here is understood as belonging to the survivors. Keil and Delitzsch describe a church now refined by the judgment and rejoicing in its calling to the whole world, with the majesty of God as both ground and subject of the rejoicing. Henry finds the comfort in the geography: the saints may be driven to the uttermost parts of the earth by the calamities of the places they lived in, or forced there for their religion, and yet what is heard from those regions is singing rather than sighing, which is itself evidence that they carried their religion with them and that God visits them there. Gill hears in the songs a thanksgiving for judgments executed and for a gospel spread through the world.

One word in the summons is contested four ways, and its form is that of the stones in the high priest's breastplate. Gill notes the sense of lights, and reports renderings that give doctrines, or valleys, or the holes and clefts of rock where the persecuted fled, before settling for the fires of affliction; Wesley reads it the same way, as the furnace of affliction. Clarke prefers to emend, reading isles rather than valleys, which he thinks justified by the repetition of the word in the following clause with the sea added, exactly in the prophet's manner; he lists half a dozen further conjectures by others and notes that the Greek expresses only islands.

Ellicott sets out three interpretations and chooses the one nobody else takes. Read as light, the word means the east, set against the isles of the sea as the west, so the whole is a form of the familiar phrase from the rising of the sun to its going down; he supports this from Assyrian inscriptions and a Greek poet's use of the dawn for the East, and prefers it as truer to the primary meaning and giving the more vivid antithesis. Calvin takes the valleys and makes something unexpected of them: countries shut in by mountains are separated by nature, their inhabitants less civilised for having fewer opportunities of conversing with each other, so the sense is that no corner will be too obscure for the praises of God to be heard in it.

What the song itself says then divides them evenly. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the righteous one can be God, since he is never so called in this absolute way, and refer the phrase instead to the church of righteous men. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion on two grounds: the word rendered glory is not the one used in doxologies but rather honour, such as is applied to men, and the title is never used absolutely of God. He would render it honour to the righteous, meaning the true Israel as a righteous people. Henry takes it the other way, noting the word is singular and may refer to the righteous God, who is just in all he has brought upon us; Wesley agrees, glossing it the Lord, the righteous one.

The turn at the end of the verse is abrupt and all of them feel it. Ellicott describes the prophet as recalled from the ideal to the actual, from the glory of the future to the misery of the present, and notes that leanness was the natural symbol of extremest sorrow. Calvin puts the difficulty plainly: the verse contains two statements with some appearance of being at variance, opening with a joyful description of God's praises and passing straight to lamentation over the treachery of those who overturn religion. Clarke reports a different sense from the Aramaic, my secret rather than my leanness, and remarks on the strange succession of uncouth sounds the Hebrew makes here. Wesley takes the treachery for that of the prophet's own people, repeated to show the horridness of the crime.
17:
The three words of the threat form a hunting sequence, and all who take it up say so. Gill notes the play of sound, three near-identical Hebrew words that cannot well be carried into English, and the allusion to creatures that flee in fear, fall into pits and are entangled in snares. Ellicott describes the same succession: the terror of the startled beast, the pit dug for him, the snare waiting if he struggled out. Clarke supplies the machinery from ancient practice: the terror was a line strung with coloured feathers which fluttered and drove the beasts into the toils, the pit was dug deep and covered with boughs and turf, and the snare was a series of nets thrown round a wide space and drawn in by degrees. Both note that a later prophet reproduced the phrase against Moab.

The threefold naming of the earth in the next verse is heard as deliberate. Ellicott makes the finest observation in the chapter, that the three clauses form a climax representing the three stages of an earthquake, the first cleavage of the ground, the wide open gaping, and the final shattering convulsion, and that the rhythm of the passage is almost an echo of the crashes. Wesley takes the repetition more simply, as showing the dreadfulness and certainty of the judgments and awakening a stupid people. Calvin generalises it into a theory of prophetic style: the prophets adorn their language and heap up figures, not because they cared to be thought eloquent, but to make sluggish hearers attentive and sting them to the quick.

The two similes for the reeling earth are handled differently. Gill applies the drunkenness to the inhabitants and finds a retaliation in it, since having been drunk with sin and having drunk up iniquity like water they are now made drunk with punishment. Clarke renders the second figure a lodge for a night. Ellicott would make it a hammock, a hanging mat slung from a tree in which the keeper of a vineyard slept, moving with every breath of wind and so the very type of instability. Calvin refuses to take either figure physically: no change is meant in the earth's position, and the words must be referred to men, the sense being that no kingly power and no regular government would be left.

What makes the earth fall is its own weight, and Calvin builds his best argument of the chapter on that. The prophet assigns the iniquity as the reason, he says, that we may understand God is never angry without a cause, since we are ourselves the authors of all the evils we suffer; God is by nature disposed to kindness and regards us with a father's love, so it is our own fault if we are treated with severity. Ellicott reaches the same clause by another road, noting that the Hebrew pictures the world as resting on pillars, so that a world tottering under the weight of its guilt falls and does not rise again.

The host of the high ones divides them three ways. Ellicott finds the utterance growing more apocalyptic and takes the punishment to reach the principalities and powers in heavenly places, perhaps identified with the gods the nations worshipped; he holds the parallelism of the two clauses decisive against reading the high ones as merely earthly. Clarke takes precisely that rejected view, understanding the ecclesiastical and civil polity of his own nation. Calvin reports that the passage has tortured many commentators, lists the readings making it the stars, the devils, or the Jews, refuses all, and offers instead that no power is high enough to escape, since though they rise above the clouds God's hand will reach them. Keil and Delitzsch keep both, holding that punishment must fall at once on the princes of heaven and of earth.
